titulo.texto: Structure 4: A Platform Seventy Meters Long

frase_gancho.texto: A platform about seventy meters long, elite burials nearby, and an open question: where Monument Nine came from.

puente_narrativo.texto: Follow your route: the story of this platform continues in other stones of the settlement.

guion_corto.texto: About seventy meters. That is the scale of Structure Four, one of the largest platforms at the site. The sources do not agree on its exact shape, but they do agree on its size. Its earliest stages go back to the Amate phase, the oldest in the Chalcatzingo sequence. Nearby, elite burials were found with jade objects and magnetite mirrors. These materials came from far away and marked rank. David Grove proposed that Monument Nine, the Portal to the Underworld you saw in the museum, was erected on this platform. The sources do not agree on its shape, but they do agree on its scale. It is a hypothesis, not a certainty.

guion_largo.texto:
A platform seventy meters long is not raised in a day. Structure Four is one of the largest constructions at Chalcatzingo, and its history is told in stages.

Let us begin with the size. According to the official INAH record, the platform measures about seventy meters per side. Grove describes it as a platform about seventy meters long and seven high. The two sources do not agree on the shape, so hold on to the scale: it is an enormous volume for a town more than two thousand five hundred years ago.

It is also one of the oldest parts of the site. Its early stages belong to the Amate phase, the first in the sequence that archaeologists have reconstructed. Over time the platform grew, and that is why we speak of stages.

A platform like this is a base of earth and stone on which buildings were raised or ceremonies were held. The sources consulted do not say what stood on top of this one.

According to Grove, the Amate phase runs from fifteen hundred to eleven hundred years before Christ. These are uncalibrated radiocarbon dates, that is, approximate ones. If the first stages belong to that phase, they are several centuries older than the terraces and the reliefs you will see further on. For a people of that time, moving so much earth and stone was a collective task.

The fact that the burials are near the platform suggests that the place was important to certain families. The sources consulted do not say who they were.

Open questions remain. We do not know in detail what the platform was used for in each stage, or when it stopped being used. The sources we consulted do not specify it, and we prefer to say so rather than invent it.

Nearby, burials appeared with jade objects and magnetite mirrors. Jade is one of the green stones that Grove mentions when he explains why Chalcatzingo connected with nearby and distant regions. Emerging elites sought those exotic materials. A magnetite mirror is a polished piece of a dark mineral that reflects light like a mirror.

Arqueología Mexicana explains, regarding another site in Morelos, that in those centuries Mesoamerican societies were shifting from egalitarian to stratified. One part of the group separated from the rest and became the dominant stratum. Burials with materials like these are understood in that context.

There is another reason to stop here. Grove suggested that [Monument Nine](chz_02_museo_portal_inframundo) was erected on this great platform, at its northern edge. INAH, in two thousand twenty-five, proposes another possibility: that it was part of the program of the hill. There is no way to decide between the two with what is known today.

Imagine, then, the whole ensemble. A platform seventy meters long to the north, an elite residence to the south, a broad plaza in the middle. It is the image of a power built with earth and stone, and displayed to everyone who crosses the plaza.

texto: Walk along the platform and estimate how many steps it measures
Look at its size from the plaza
Imagine Monument Nine standing at its edge

texto.pregunta: Myth: It is a natural hill.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a platform built in stages, about seventy meters long.
